dropped.reason: Not in 2017 syllabus: forming a polyamide from a diamide with loss of ammonia (syllabus condensation polymers form from amine/hydroxyl and carboxyl groups with loss of water); the question's premise is chemically unsound

questions.question: Which diagram represents ionisation of a weak acid? (See the key: open circles with two dots are water molecules; shaded circles with one dot are molecules of the weak acid.)
questions.answer: A weak acid only partially ionises, so the solution should contain mostly un-ionised acid molecules with only a few $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and $\text{A}^-$ ions. Diagram C shows this. (A shows complete ionisation — a strong acid; B and D show no ionisation.)

questions.question:
Increasing amounts of carbon dioxide were dissolved in two beakers, one containing water and one a mixture of water and a buffer. The pH in each beaker was measured and the results graphed.

Which graph best represents the results?
questions.answer: Dissolved $\text{CO}_2$ forms carbonic acid, so the pH of water falls steadily. The buffer resists the change in pH, so its pH stays almost constant at first and only falls sharply once the buffer's capacity is exceeded — graph A.

questions.question: Which combination of equimolar solutions would produce the most basic mixture?
questions.answer: Equal amounts of acetic acid (monoprotic, weak) and $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ (strong base, provides 2 $\text{OH}^-$) leave half the hydroxide in excess, and the conjugate base $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ is also basic. The other combinations either neutralise exactly (C) or involve the much weaker base carbonate and/or the diprotic strong acid, giving a less basic (or acidic) mixture.

questions.question:
The graph shows the pH of a solution of a weak acid, HA, as a function of temperature.

What happens as the temperature decreases?
options: HA becomes less ionised and the $\text{H}^+$ concentration increases.
HA becomes less ionised and the $\text{H}^+$ concentration decreases.
HA becomes more ionised and the $\text{H}^+$ concentration increases.
HA becomes more ionised and the $\text{H}^+$ concentration decreases.
questions.answer: As temperature decreases the pH rises, so $[\text{H}^+]$ decreases. Since the acid concentration is unchanged, less HA has ionised.

questions.question:
Which indicator would be best for distinguishing between lemon juice (pH = 2.3) and potato juice (pH = 5.8)?

| Indicator | Colour at different pH | |
|---|---|---|
| (A) Crystal violet | 0.2 – yellow | 1.8 – blue |
| (B) Methyl orange | 3.2 – red | 4.4 – yellow |
| (C) Bromothymol blue | 6.0 – yellow | 7.6 – blue |
| (D) Phenolphthalein | 8.2 – colourless | 10.0 – pink |
questions.answer: The indicator must change colour between pH 2.3 and 5.8. Methyl orange is red at pH 2.3 and yellow at pH 5.8. Crystal violet would be blue for both, bromothymol blue yellow for both and phenolphthalein colourless for both.

questions.question:
Chlorine gas ($\text{Cl}_2$) and carbon monoxide gas (CO) are placed into a sealed container and kept at a temperature of 25 °C. Phosgene gas ($\text{COCl}_2$) is produced as follows:
$$\text{Cl}_2(g) + \text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{COCl}_2(g)$$
Which statement about this reaction is correct?
options: All the $\text{Cl}_2$ and CO will be converted into $\text{COCl}_2$
At a temperature of 25 °C the $\text{COCl}_2$ will not form
The forward reaction will continue to occur until the concentration of $\text{COCl}_2$ remains constant
When the forward and reverse reactions become equal the concentration of the $\text{COCl}_2$ becomes constant
questions.answer: In a closed system dynamic equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations then remain constant. (The forward reaction does not stop — C — and the conversion is not complete — A.)

questions.question:
An equilibrium reaction is carried out at two different temperatures – $T_1$ and $T_2$. The concentration of the product gas X is recorded over time.

Based on this graph, which of the following statements is correct?
options: A greater concentration of gas X is constantly produced for temperature $T_1$.
Equilibrium is achieved at the same time for both temperatures.
The initial rate of reaction is greater for temperature $T_1$ than $T_2$.
Temperature $T_2$ is definitely higher than temperature $T_1$.
questions.answer: The initial gradient of the $T_1$ curve is steeper and it reaches equilibrium sooner, so the initial rate is greater at $T_1$. (Whether $T_2$ is higher depends on whether the reaction is endo- or exothermic, which is not given.)

questions.question:
Consider the following equilibrium.
$$\text{HA}(aq) + \text{B}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{A}^-(aq) + \text{HB}(aq) \qquad K_{eq} = 2.5$$
Which row correctly identifies the weakest acid and the strongest base in the equilibrium?
questions.answer: $K_{eq} > 1$, so products are favoured: HA donates protons more readily than HB, and $\text{B}^-$ accepts protons more readily than $\text{A}^-$. So HB is the weaker acid and $\text{B}^-$ the stronger base.

questions.question:
Three gases L, M and N in a sealed 5.0 L container react to form an equilibrium. The graph shows how the concentration of these gases changes at time $t_1$ when the mixture is heated.

Which is correct for the reaction in this graph?
options: $\text{L}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{M}(g) + \text{N}(g)$ and the forward reaction is exothermic
$2\text{M}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{L}(g) + \text{N}(g)$ and the forward reaction is endothermic
$2\text{M}(g) + \text{N}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{L}(g)$ and the forward reaction is exothermic
$\text{L}(g) + 2\text{M}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{N}(g)$ and the forward reaction is endothermic
questions.answer: On heating, [M] falls by about 0.4, [N] by 0.2 and [L] rises by 0.2 mol L$^{-1}$, so M and N are converted to L in a 2 : 1 : 1 ratio: the reaction that occurs is $2\text{M} + \text{N} \rightarrow \text{L}$, which must be endothermic (favoured by heating). Written as $\text{L} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{M} + \text{N}$, the forward reaction is therefore exothermic — A. (C has the right equation but the wrong sign of $\Delta H$.)

questions.question:
A particular reaction can occur with or without a catalyst. The energy profile of this reaction, both catalysed (dashed) and uncatalysed (solid), is shown.

Which row best matches the reaction as shown by the energy profile? (Values in kJ mol$^{-1}$.)
options: $E_a$ uncatalysed $-80$; $\Delta H$ uncatalysed $70$; $E_a$ catalysed $-60$; $\Delta H$ catalysed $70$
$E_a$ uncatalysed $80$; $\Delta H$ uncatalysed $-150$; $E_a$ catalysed $80$; $\Delta H$ catalysed $60$
$E_a$ uncatalysed $80$; $\Delta H$ uncatalysed $-70$; $E_a$ catalysed $60$; $\Delta H$ catalysed $-70$
$E_a$ uncatalysed $20$; $\Delta H$ uncatalysed $80$; $E_a$ catalysed $150$; $\Delta H$ catalysed $-80$
questions.answer: Reactants are at 0, products at about $-70$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, so $\Delta H = -70$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ for both (a catalyst doesn't change $\Delta H$). The peaks are at 80 (uncatalysed) and 60 (catalysed) kJ mol$^{-1}$ above the reactants, giving those activation energies.

questions.question:
Hydrogen and iodine react according to the following equilibrium reaction. $$\text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{HI}(g) \qquad \Delta H < 0$$ A mixture of hydrogen gas and iodine gas was placed in a container, sealed and allowed to reach equilibrium. Changes were made to the mixture and the mole amounts of reactants and product were measured. I. The volume of the container was increased with the temperature remaining constant.
II. Hydrogen gas was added to the container with the volume and temperature remaining constant.
III. An inert gas was added to the container with the volume increasing and temperature remaining constant.
IV. The temperature of the gases was decreased with the volume remaining constant. Which changes would result in an increase in the number of moles of hydrogen iodide formed?
questions.answer: There are 2 mol of gas on each side, so changing volume (I, III) has no effect on the position of equilibrium. Adding $\text{H}_2$ (II) shifts the equilibrium right, and lowering the temperature (IV) favours the exothermic forward reaction. Both increase n(HI).

questions.question: Which diagram best shows the main equipment required to isolate a pure sample of a prepared synthetic ester?
questions.answer: B is a distillation set-up (flask, still head with thermometer, condenser and receiver), used to separate the ester from the reaction mixture by boiling point. A is reflux apparatus, used for the reaction itself, not isolation.

questions.question: What is the systematic name for this compound?
questions.answer: The longest chain has 6 carbons (hexane). Numbering from the end nearest the substituents puts methyl groups on C2 and C3 and Cl on C3; substituents are listed alphabetically: 3-chloro-2,3-dimethylhexane.

questions.question:
Designing industrial synthesis processes to maximise the number of reactions that have a high 'atom economy' is one aim of 'green chemistry', a movement towards lowering the environmental impact of the chemical industry and the products it creates.

*The atom economy for a chemical reaction is a measure of the amount of atoms from the starting materials that are present in the useful products at the end of the reaction. Having a high atom economy means any by-products of a reaction, which may not have a significant use, are minimised.*

Of the general reactions below, which would have the highest atom economy?
options: Addition of bromine to an alkene.
Substitution of an alkane by reaction with a halogen.
questions.answer: In an addition reaction all atoms of both reactants end up in a single product (100% atom economy). Elimination produces water, hydrolysis gives two products, and substitution produces HX as a by-product.

questions.question:
Ethers are a family of organic compounds which contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. The oxygen atom in an ether is joined to carbon atoms on either side by single bonds, as shown in the example of dimethyl ether in the table below. Some information about dimethyl ether and ethanol is also shown in the table.

Which explanation best accounts for the differences in the properties of dimethyl ether and ethanol shown in the table?
options: Ethanol molecules are more polar than dimethyl ether molecules.
The hydrogen bonds in ethanol are stronger than those in dimethyl ether.
The hydrogen bonding is more extensive in ethanol than in dimethyl ether.
The O–H bonds in ethanol are stronger than the C–O bonds in dimethyl ether.
questions.answer:
Ethanol has an O–H group, so its molecules hydrogen bond to each other and form extensive hydrogen bonds with water. Dimethyl ether has no O–H, so there is no hydrogen bonding between its molecules (it can only accept hydrogen bonds from water), giving a much lower boiling point and lower solubility. Polarity differences (A) are small and do not explain the large differences.

*Note: the paper's answer key gives A; C is the better explanation, since the differences arise from hydrogen bonding rather than overall polarity.*

questions.question: Which isomer of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$ would show three signals in its $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR spectrum?
questions.answer: B, 1-methylethyl methanoate $\text{HCOOCH(CH}_3)_2$, has three carbon environments: the C=O carbon, the CH carbon and the two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ carbons. A (ethyl ethanoate) and D have 4 environments; C is symmetrical and has only 2.

questions.question:
The structural formulae of five organic compounds, labelled A–E, are shown below.

Which alternative identifies a pair of these compounds which are examples of each type of structural isomer?

| | Chain isomers | Functional group isomers | Position isomers |
|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | C and E | A and C | B and D |
| (B) | C and D | C and E | A and B |
| (C) | A and C | C and E | B and D |
| (D) | C and E | C and D | A and B |
questions.answer:
All five are $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$. A = methyl propanoate, B = ethyl ethanoate, C = 2-methylpropanoic acid, D = propyl methanoate, E = butanoic acid.
- Chain isomers (same group, different carbon skeleton): C and E (both acids).
- Functional group isomers: an acid with an ester, e.g. C and D (or A and C).
- Position isomers (ester linkage in a different position): A and B (or B and D).

Row D fits; row A also fits on the same reasoning. B and C are wrong because C/D and A/C are not chain isomers.

*Note: the paper's key gives "B & D"; row B is incorrect (C and D are functional group isomers, not chain isomers) — the two acceptable rows are A and D.*

questions.question:
A sample of Teflon, polytetrafluoroethene, was found to have a molecular mass of $1.9 \times 10^{4}$ g mol$^{-1}$.

On average, how many monomer units are there in the polymer?
questions.answer: Monomer $\text{C}_2\text{F}_4$: $M = 2(12.01) + 4(19.00) = 100.0$ g mol$^{-1}$. Number of units $= \dfrac{1.9 \times 10^4}{100.0} \approx 190$.

questions.question: Which pieces of glassware should be used when preparing a primary standard solution?
options: Beaker, filter funnel and volumetric flask
Measuring cylinder, stirring rod and conical flask
questions.answer: The weighed solid is dissolved in a beaker, transferred through a filter funnel into a volumetric flask and made up accurately to the mark.

questions.question:
The structure shown below represents a fragment of a polymer made from two different monomers.

Which option is correct with respect to the synthesis of this polymer?
questions.answer: The chain is joined by ester linkages formed between a dicarboxylic acid and a diol, so it is a condensation polymer (polyester), and a small molecule (water) is eliminated for each linkage formed.

questions.question:
A chemist is analysing an unknown organic compound with the molecular formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$. The following observations are made:
1. The compound does not decolorise a solution of bromine in dichloromethane.
2. The compound is treated with acidified potassium permanganate, which results in the formation of a carboxylic acid.

Based on the reaction with bromine, what can be inferred about the presence of a double bond in the compound?
questions.answer: The compound does not decolourise bromine, so it does not contain a carbon–carbon double (or triple) bond — it is saturated (not an alkene).

questions.question:
A chemist is analysing an unknown organic compound with the molecular formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$. The following observations are made:
1. The compound does not decolorise a solution of bromine in dichloromethane.
2. The compound is treated with acidified potassium permanganate, which results in the formation of a carboxylic acid.

Based on the reaction with acidified potassium permanganate, what functional group is present in the compound?
questions.answer: A hydroxyl group as part of a **primary alcohol** ($-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) — primary alcohols are oxidised by acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ to carboxylic acids.

questions.question:
A chemist is analysing an unknown organic compound with the molecular formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$. The following observations are made:
1. The compound does not decolorise a solution of bromine in dichloromethane.
2. The compound is treated with acidified potassium permanganate, which results in the formation of a carboxylic acid.

Propose a structure for the compound.
questions.answer: Propan-1-ol: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, a three-carbon saturated chain with the –OH on the end carbon. (It is oxidised to propanoic acid.)

questions.question: Draw the structural formula and give the systematic name of the major product of the dehydration of the compound shown below.
questions.answer:
Dehydration removes the –OH and an H from an adjacent carbon. C2 carries no hydrogen (it is bonded to three methyl groups), so the H must come from C4 and the double bond forms between C3 and C4:
$$(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}{-}\text{CH}{=}\text{CH}{-}\text{CH}_2{-}\text{CH}_3$$
Name: **2,2-dimethylhex-3-ene**.

questions.question: Sodium dihydrogen phosphate is an amphiprotic salt. Explain what is meant by the term 'amphiprotic'. Support your answer with chemical equations.
questions.answer:
An amphiprotic species can both donate a proton (act as a Brønsted–Lowry acid) and accept a proton (act as a Brønsted–Lowry base), depending on what it reacts with.

The dihydrogen phosphate ion, $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$, from $\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4$:

As an acid (donating a proton to water):
$$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HPO}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$
As a base (accepting a proton from water):
$$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq)$$

questions.question:
Carbon monoxide (CO) is a poisonous and flammable gas that is used in the separation of metals from their oxides. It may be produced in the following manner.
$$\text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$$
At 600 °C, 1.40 moles of carbon dioxide gas react with 1.0 mole of hydrogen gas in a 2.0 litre reaction vessel. At equilibrium, the vessel was found to contain 0.88 moles of carbon dioxide and 0.48 moles of hydrogen.

Use a correct expression to calculate the equilibrium constant ($K_{eq}$) for this reaction and state what this indicates about the production of carbon monoxide gas at this temperature.
questions.answer:
$$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{CO}_2][\text{H}_2]}$$
(All species are gases, so $\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$ is included.)

Amount of $\text{CO}_2$ reacted $= 1.40 - 0.88 = 0.52$ mol (and $1.0 - 0.48 = 0.52$ mol $\text{H}_2$), so 0.52 mol each of CO and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ form.

| | $[\text{CO}_2]$ | $[\text{H}_2]$ | $[\text{CO}]$ | $[\text{H}_2\text{O}]$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Initial | 0.70 | 0.50 | 0 | 0 |
| Change | −0.26 | −0.26 | +0.26 | +0.26 |
| Equilibrium | 0.44 | 0.24 | 0.26 | 0.26 |

(concentrations in mol L$^{-1}$, dividing moles by 2.0 L)
$$K_{eq} = \frac{(0.26)(0.26)}{(0.44)(0.24)} = 0.64$$
Since $K_{eq} < 1$, at equilibrium the reactants are favoured: the equilibrium lies to the left, so the production of carbon monoxide is not favoured at this temperature (only a modest yield of CO is obtained).

questions.question:
1.00 gram of lead(II) nitrate is dissolved in distilled water. The solution is made up to a volume of 100.0 mL. It is then added to 100.0 mL of a 0.001 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of potassium iodide. The reaction takes place at 25 °C.

Write a net ionic equation for this investigation and predict whether a precipitate would form when the two solutions are mixed. Include all calculations in your answer. ($K_{sp}(\text{PbI}_2) = 9.8 \times 10^{-9}$ at 25 °C.)
questions.answer:
Net ionic equation:
$$\text{Pb}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{I}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{PbI}_2(s)$$
$M(\text{Pb(NO}_3)_2) = 207.2 + 2(14.01) + 6(16.00) = 331.2$ g mol$^{-1}$

$n(\text{Pb}^{2+}) = \dfrac{1.00}{331.2} = 3.02 \times 10^{-3}$ mol; in the total 200.0 mL: $[\text{Pb}^{2+}] = \dfrac{3.02 \times 10^{-3}}{0.2000} = 0.0151$ mol L$^{-1}$

$n(\text{I}^-) = 0.001 \times 0.1000 = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}$ mol; $[\text{I}^-] = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-4}}{0.2000} = 5.0 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$

$$Q = [\text{Pb}^{2+}][\text{I}^-]^2 = 0.0151 \times (5.0 \times 10^{-4})^2 = 3.8 \times 10^{-9}$$
$Q = 3.8 \times 10^{-9} < K_{sp} = 9.8 \times 10^{-9}$, so the solution is not saturated and **no precipitate will form**.

questions.question:
A coffee cup calorimeter (shown) was used by a student to measure the enthalpy of neutralisation of an acid–base reaction.

120 mL of 0.500 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide was added to 60.0 mL of 0.500 mol L$^{-1}$ sulfuric acid. Both solutions were at a temperature of 24.2 °C. After mixing, the final temperature was 26.3 °C.

Calculate the enthalpy change per mole of water formed in this reaction.
questions.answer:
$$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + 2\text{NaOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
$n(\text{NaOH}) = 0.500 \times 0.120 = 0.0600$ mol; $n(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4) = 0.500 \times 0.0600 = 0.0300$ mol — exactly the 1 : 2 ratio, so $n(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = n(\text{NaOH}) = 0.0600$ mol.

Mass of solution $\approx 120 + 60.0 = 180$ g (density ≈ 1 g mL$^{-1}$), $\Delta T = 26.3 - 24.2 = 2.1$ °C:
$$q = mc\Delta T = 180 \times 4.18 \times 2.1 = 1.58 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J} = 1.58\ \text{kJ}$$
$$\Delta H = -\frac{q}{n(\text{H}_2\text{O})} = -\frac{1.58}{0.0600} = -26\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
(−26.3 kJ mol$^{-1}$; negative because the reaction is exothermic.)

questions.question:
A colourimeter with an orange filter was used to analyse the concentration of copper ions in a solution. To calibrate the colourimeter, a distilled water blank and eight standards of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ were prepared. Their absorbances were measured to give the calibration curve shown.

A 20.0 mL sample of a copper solution of unknown concentration was diluted to a total volume of 80.0 mL. This diluted solution recorded an absorbance of 0.500.

Use the graph to determine the mass of the copper ions contained in the 20.0 mL sample.
questions.answer:
Draw the line of best fit through the standards (passing through the origin). Reading across from absorbance 0.500 to the line and down gives $[\text{Cu}^{2+}] \approx 0.0300$ mol L$^{-1}$ in the **diluted** solution.

All the copper in the 20.0 mL sample is now in the 80.0 mL of diluted solution:
$$n(\text{Cu}^{2+}) = cV = 0.0300 \times 0.0800 = 2.40 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$$
$$m(\text{Cu}^{2+}) = nM = 2.40 \times 10^{-3} \times 63.55 = 0.153\ \text{g}$$

questions.question:
A student wanted to determine the concentration of a solution of potassium hydroxide. They did this by reacting a 25 mL aliquot with a standard solution of hydrochloric acid while measuring the conductivity of the solution. 10.00 mL volumes of 0.1012 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid were incrementally added using a burette and the conductivity was measured after each addition. The student recorded the data shown in the graph.

Explain the trend shown in the graph.
questions.answer:
Conductivity depends on the concentration (and mobility) of ions in solution.
- **Decrease (0 to ≈55 mL):** added $\text{H}^+$ reacts with $\text{OH}^-$ ($\text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}$). Highly mobile $\text{OH}^-$ ions are removed and replaced by less mobile $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, so conductivity falls.
- **Minimum (≈55 mL):** the lowest conductivity is the equivalence point — all the $\text{OH}^-$ has been neutralised and only $\text{K}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ remain.
- **Increase (after ≈55 mL):** excess HCl adds highly mobile $\text{H}^+$ (and $\text{Cl}^-$) ions that are no longer neutralised, so the concentration of ions and the conductivity rise.

questions.question:
A student wanted to determine the concentration of a solution of potassium hydroxide. They did this by reacting a 25 mL aliquot with a standard solution of hydrochloric acid while measuring the conductivity of the solution. 10.00 mL volumes of 0.1012 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid were incrementally added using a burette and the conductivity was measured after each addition. The student recorded the data shown in the graph.

Calculate the concentration of the potassium hydroxide solution.
questions.answer:
From the graph the equivalence point (minimum conductivity) is at about 55 mL of HCl.
$$\text{HCl}(aq) + \text{KOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{KCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
$n(\text{HCl}) = 0.1012 \times 0.055 = 5.57 \times 10^{-3}$ mol $= n(\text{KOH})$ (1 : 1)
$$[\text{KOH}] = \frac{5.57 \times 10^{-3}}{0.025} = 0.22\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

questions.question:
Isobutanol, shown below, has been investigated as a possible fuel source for internal combustion engines.

Give the IUPAC name for the structure shown.
questions.answer: 2-methylpropan-1-ol

questions.question:
Isobutanol, shown below, has been investigated as a possible fuel source for internal combustion engines.

Outline a procedure which could be used to estimate the heat of combustion of this fuel in a typical school laboratory. Include a labelled diagram of the apparatus used as well as a justified safety precaution for this type of investigation.
questions.answer:
Apparatus (see diagram): spirit burner containing isobutanol under a metal (copper) can of water held by a clamp on a retort stand, with a thermometer in the water; a draught shield/foil around the can.

Procedure:
1. Measure a known mass of water (e.g. 200 g) into the copper can and record its initial temperature $T_i$.
2. Weigh the spirit burner containing isobutanol (with its cap) on an electronic balance: $m_1$.
3. Clamp the can a short, fixed distance above the wick; surround with a draught shield/aluminium foil to minimise heat loss to the surroundings.
4. Light the burner and stir the water gently until its temperature has risen by about 10–20 °C, then extinguish the flame (replace the cap) and record the highest temperature $T_f$.
5. Reweigh the burner: $m_2$. Mass of fuel burnt $= m_1 - m_2$.
6. Calculate $q = m_{\text{water}}c(T_f - T_i)$, $n(\text{fuel}) = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{74.12}$ and $\Delta H_c = -\dfrac{q}{n}$ (J mol$^{-1}$). Repeat to improve reliability.

Safety: isobutanol is flammable — keep the fuel bottle capped and away from the flame, refill the burner only when it is cool and unlit, and wipe up any spills so no unexpected flames occur; wear safety glasses.

questions.question:
Butan-2-ol is an isomer of isobutanol (2-methylpropan-1-ol). Data from the mass spectra of the two compounds are shown in the table below.

| Compound | Parent ion peak ($m/z$) | Base peak ($m/z$) |
|---|---|---|
| Isobutanol | 74 | 43 |
| Butan-2-ol | 74 | 45 |

Explain a similarity and a difference between the two spectra.
questions.answer:
**Similarity:** both compounds have the molecular formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ and so the same molar mass (74 g mol$^{-1}$); the molecular (parent) ion $[\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}]^+$ appears at $m/z = 74$ in both spectra.

**Difference:** the compounds have different structures, so they fragment differently and give different base peaks (most abundant fragment).
- Isobutanol, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}{-}\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, breaks to form the stable $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$ fragment, $m/z = 43$.
- Butan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}{-}\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, breaks next to the C–OH carbon to form $\text{CH}_3\text{CHOH}^+$, $m/z = 45$.

questions.question:
Carbonyl chloride ($\text{COCl}_2$) gas can be formed in an equilibrium reaction between carbon monoxide (CO) gas and chlorine ($\text{Cl}_2$) gas:
$$\text{CO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{COCl}_2(g)$$
A 10 L vessel containing these gases, but not at equilibrium, was sampled. It was found that there were 0.11 moles of carbon monoxide, 0.63 moles of chlorine and 2.9 moles of carbonyl chloride present in the vessel. The equilibrium constant ($K_{eq}$) for this reaction, under the conditions used, is $2.62 \times 10^{2}$.

Write the equilibrium expression for this reaction.
questions.answer: $$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{COCl}_2]}{[\text{CO}][\text{Cl}_2]}$$

questions.question:
Carbonyl chloride ($\text{COCl}_2$) gas can be formed in an equilibrium reaction between carbon monoxide (CO) gas and chlorine ($\text{Cl}_2$) gas:
$$\text{CO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{COCl}_2(g)$$
A 10 L vessel containing these gases, but not at equilibrium, was sampled. It was found that there were 0.11 moles of carbon monoxide, 0.63 moles of chlorine and 2.9 moles of carbonyl chloride present in the vessel. The equilibrium constant ($K_{eq}$) for this reaction, under the conditions used, is $2.62 \times 10^{2}$.

After sampling, in which direction will the reaction shift in order to reach equilibrium? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
Concentrations (dividing by 10 L): $[\text{CO}] = 0.011$, $[\text{Cl}_2] = 0.063$, $[\text{COCl}_2] = 0.29$ mol L$^{-1}$.
$$Q = \frac{[\text{COCl}_2]}{[\text{CO}][\text{Cl}_2]} = \frac{0.29}{(0.011)(0.063)} = 4.2 \times 10^{2}$$
$Q\ (4.2 \times 10^2) > K_{eq}\ (2.62 \times 10^2)$, so the system is not at equilibrium and there are too many products relative to reactants. Q must decrease, which happens when $\text{COCl}_2$ decomposes and CO and $\text{Cl}_2$ increase — the reverse reaction is favoured and the equilibrium shifts to the **left**.

questions.question:
Carbonyl chloride ($\text{COCl}_2$) gas is formed in the equilibrium
$$\text{CO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{COCl}_2(g)$$
A mixture of carbon monoxide, chlorine and carbonyl chloride was allowed to come to equilibrium. The rate of reaction was monitored at a constant temperature. The diagram shows the rate of formation of carbonyl chloride over a period of time. At $t_1$ the volume of the reaction vessel was decreased.

Explain, using collision theory, the shape of the graph over time. Refer to any factors that affect the rate of reaction in your answer.
questions.answer:
The rate of formation of $\text{COCl}_2$ depends on the frequency of successful collisions between CO and $\text{Cl}_2$ particles (with energy ≥ $E_a$ and correct orientation).
- **Before $t_1$:** the system is at equilibrium, concentrations are constant, so the collision frequency and the forward rate are constant (horizontal line).
- **At $t_1$:** decreasing the volume increases the pressure and the concentrations of all gases. CO and $\text{Cl}_2$ particles are closer together and collide more frequently, so the forward rate increases suddenly (vertical rise).
- **$t_1$ to $t_2$:** by Le Chatelier's principle the system shifts to the side with fewer gas particles ($\text{COCl}_2$, 1 mol vs 2 mol). As CO and $\text{Cl}_2$ are consumed their concentrations fall, collisions become less frequent and the forward rate gradually decreases, while the reverse rate increases, until the rates are equal again.
- **After $t_2$:** a new equilibrium is established (horizontal line). The new forward rate is higher than before $t_1$ because the shift only partially counteracts the change — [CO] and [$\text{Cl}_2$] remain higher than at the original equilibrium.

questions.question:
The following table shows four acids which were tested for relative conductivity and pH:

| Acid tested | Relative conductivity | pH |
|---|---|---|
| Concentrated $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ (100% pure), known as glacial acetic acid | Does not conduct | Unable to measure |
| 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ HCl solution | high | 1.0 |
| 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ solution | moderate | 3.3 |
| 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ solution | high | 0.7 |

Explain why the pH for glacial acetic acid is unable to be measured.
questions.answer: pH measures the concentration of $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ ions, and an acid only produces ions when it ionises in water ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$). Glacial acetic acid is pure covalent molecular $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ with no water present, so it does not ionise: there are essentially no free ions, so it does not conduct and no $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$/pH can be measured.

questions.question:
The following table shows four acids which were tested for relative conductivity and pH:

| Acid tested | Relative conductivity | pH |
|---|---|---|
| Concentrated $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ (100% pure), known as glacial acetic acid | Does not conduct | Unable to measure |
| 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ HCl solution | high | 1.0 |
| 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ solution | moderate | 3.3 |
| 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ solution | high | 0.7 |

Explain the differences in the pH values for the 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ acids that were tested. Include relevant calculations.
questions.answer:
pH depends on $[\text{H}^+]$, which depends on the strength of the acid (degree of ionisation) and the number of ionisable protons.

**HCl** is a strong monoprotic acid that ionises completely: $\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq)$
$[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-1.0} = 0.10$ mol L$^{-1}$ = concentration of the acid (100% ionised).

**$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$** is a strong diprotic acid; it can release two protons per molecule: $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{H}^+(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)$
$[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-0.7} = 0.20$ mol L$^{-1}$ — about twice that of HCl at the same concentration, so its pH is lower (0.7). It is not a "stronger" acid than HCl; it has more ionisable protons.

**$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$** is a weak monoprotic acid that only partially ionises: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq) + \text{H}^+(aq)$
$[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-3.3} = 5.0 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$, so only $\dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{-4}}{0.1} \times 100 = 0.5\%$ of the molecules are ionised. The much lower $[\text{H}^+]$ gives the highest pH (3.3) even though the concentration is the same.

So pH: $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (strong, diprotic) < HCl (strong, monoprotic) < $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ (weak, monoprotic), consistent with the conductivities.

questions.question:
Ethanoic acid and methanol react reversibly to form methyl ethanoate and water. The following procedure was carried out by a chemistry student to estimate the equilibrium constant for this reaction.
- A mixture weighing 8.64 g was made by adding 0.08 mol of ethanoic acid and 0.12 mol of methanol. The mixture was left in a sealed glass syringe with a sliding piston which was placed in a water bath where its temperature was held steady at 60 °C for 3 hours. After this time, the temperature of the water bath was reduced to 20 °C. The syringe was left for 24 hours in the water bath. At this point, the system was assumed to be at equilibrium.
- The contents of the syringe were thoroughly mixed to form a homogeneous mixture and 1.0 g of the mixture was measured out and titrated with 0.40 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide delivered from a burette. A mean volume of 21.20 mL of sodium hydroxide solution was needed to reach the end-point of the titration, when it was assumed all of the ethanoic acid present in the mixture had reacted with the sodium hydroxide.

Write a balanced chemical equation, using structural formulae, for the reaction between ethanoic acid and methanol which occurred in the first step of the outlined procedure.
questions.answer:
$$\text{CH}_3{-}\text{C}({=}\text{O}){-}\text{OH} + \text{HO}{-}\text{CH}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3{-}\text{C}({=}\text{O}){-}\text{O}{-}\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
ethanoic acid + methanol ⇌ methyl ethanoate + water (full structural formulae shown below).

- The contents of the syringe were thoroughly mixed to form a homogeneous mixture and 1.0 g of the mixture was measured out and titrated with 0.40 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide delivered from a burette. A mean volume of 21.20 mL of sodium hydroxide solution was needed to reach the end-point of the titration, when it was assumed all of the ethanoic acid present in the mixture had reacted with the sodium hydroxide.

Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction taking place in the titration stage of the procedure.
questions.answer: $$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{NaOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COONa}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

Ethanoic acid and methanol react reversibly to form methyl ethanoate and water. The following procedure was carried out by a chemistry student to estimate the equilibrium constant for this reaction.
- A mixture weighing 8.64 g was made by adding 0.08 mol of ethanoic acid and 0.12 mol of methanol. The mixture was left in a sealed glass syringe with a sliding piston which was placed in a water bath where its temperature was held steady at 60 °C for 3 hours. After this time, the temperature of the water bath was reduced to 20 °C. The syringe was left for 24 hours in the water bath. At this point, the system was assumed to be at equilibrium.
- The contents of the syringe were thoroughly mixed to form a homogeneous mixture and 1.0 g of the mixture was measured out and titrated with 0.40 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide delivered from a burette. A mean volume of 21.20 mL of sodium hydroxide solution was needed to reach the end-point of the titration, when it was assumed all of the ethanoic acid present in the mixture had reacted with the sodium hydroxide.

Use the data provided to calculate the number of moles of ethanoic acid remaining in the equilibrium mixture formed in the first step.
questions.answer:
$n(\text{NaOH}) = cV = 0.40 \times 0.02120 = 8.48 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$n(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})$ in the 1.0 g sample $= 8.48 \times 10^{-3}$ mol (1 : 1 ratio)

The whole mixture is 8.64 g, so
$$n(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})_{\text{total}} = 8.48 \times 10^{-3} \times \frac{8.64}{1.0} = 0.073\ \text{mol}$$

questions.question:
Ethanoic acid and methanol react reversibly to form methyl ethanoate and water. The following procedure was carried out by a chemistry student to estimate the equilibrium constant for this reaction.
- A mixture weighing 8.64 g was made by adding 0.08 mol of ethanoic acid and 0.12 mol of methanol. The mixture was left in a sealed glass syringe with a sliding piston which was placed in a water bath where its temperature was held steady at 60 °C for 3 hours. After this time, the temperature of the water bath was reduced to 20 °C. The syringe was left for 24 hours in the water bath. At this point, the system was assumed to be at equilibrium.
- The contents of the syringe were thoroughly mixed to form a homogeneous mixture and 1.0 g of the mixture was measured out and titrated with 0.40 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide delivered from a burette. A mean volume of 21.20 mL of sodium hydroxide solution was needed to reach the end-point of the titration, when it was assumed all of the ethanoic acid present in the mixture had reacted with the sodium hydroxide.

Write the expression for the equilibrium constant, $K$, for the system described by the equation for the reaction of ethanoic acid with methanol. Use molecular formulae for all species in their liquid state, including water, in the expression for $K$.
questions.answer:
$$K = \frac{[\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2][\text{CH}_4\text{O}]}$$
(equivalently $K = \dfrac{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_3][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}][\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]}$)

questions.question:
Ethanoic acid and methanol react reversibly to form methyl ethanoate and water. The following procedure was carried out by a chemistry student to estimate the equilibrium constant for this reaction.
- A mixture weighing 8.64 g was made by adding 0.08 mol of ethanoic acid and 0.12 mol of methanol. The mixture was left in a sealed glass syringe with a sliding piston which was placed in a water bath where its temperature was held steady at 60 °C for 3 hours. After this time, the temperature of the water bath was reduced to 20 °C. The syringe was left for 24 hours in the water bath. At this point, the system was assumed to be at equilibrium.
- The contents of the syringe were thoroughly mixed to form a homogeneous mixture and 1.0 g of the mixture was measured out and titrated with 0.40 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide delivered from a burette. A mean volume of 21.20 mL of sodium hydroxide solution was needed to reach the end-point of the titration, when it was assumed all of the ethanoic acid present in the mixture had reacted with the sodium hydroxide.

It was found that 0.073 mol of ethanoic acid remained in the equilibrium mixture. Use the data provided to estimate the value of $K$ for the reaction forming methyl ethanoate at 20 °C. Show all working.
questions.answer:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

| (mol) | $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ | $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ | $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_3$ | $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | 0.080 | 0.120 | 0 | 0 |
| C | −0.007 | −0.007 | +0.007 | +0.007 |
| E | 0.073 | 0.113 | 0.007 | 0.007 |

The volume cancels (2 mol of species on each side), so moles can be used directly:
$$K = \frac{(0.007)(0.007)}{(0.073)(0.113)} = \frac{4.9 \times 10^{-5}}{8.25 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 6 \times 10^{-3}$$
(Using unrounded values, 0.0733 mol acid remaining and 0.0067 mol ester, gives $K \approx 5.5 \times 10^{-3}$.)

A few drops of concentrated $	ext{H}_2	ext{SO}_4$ are often added to mixtures of an alkanol and alkanoic acid when this type of reaction is carried out in a school laboratory. What is the primary function of concentrated $	ext{H}_2	ext{SO}_4$ in this reaction?
questions.answer: It acts as a **catalyst**, increasing the rate of the esterification reaction so equilibrium is reached faster. (It is also a dehydrating agent, absorbing water and shifting the equilibrium to the right to increase the ester yield.)

questions.question:
Ethanoic acid and methanol react reversibly to form methyl ethanoate and water. The following procedure was carried out by a chemistry student to estimate the equilibrium constant for this reaction.
- A mixture weighing 8.64 g was made by adding 0.08 mol of ethanoic acid and 0.12 mol of methanol. The mixture was left in a sealed glass syringe with a sliding piston which was placed in a water bath where its temperature was held steady at 60 °C for 3 hours. After this time, the temperature of the water bath was reduced to 20 °C. The syringe was left for 24 hours in the water bath. At this point, the system was assumed to be at equilibrium.
- The contents of the syringe were thoroughly mixed to form a homogeneous mixture and 1.0 g of the mixture was measured out and titrated with 0.40 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide delivered from a burette. A mean volume of 21.20 mL of sodium hydroxide solution was needed to reach the end-point of the titration, when it was assumed all of the ethanoic acid present in the mixture had reacted with the sodium hydroxide.

Propose a chemical reason for the omission of concentrated $	ext{H}_2	ext{SO}_4$ for this particular investigation. Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: The equilibrium mixture is analysed by titration with NaOH. A catalyst is not consumed, so any $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ added would still be present and, being a strong diprotic acid, would also react with NaOH ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$). The titre would then measure total acid rather than only the remaining $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, overestimating the ethanoic acid and giving an inaccurate (too low) value of $K$. ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ would also absorb water, shifting the position of equilibrium.)

questions.question:
Ethanoic acid and methanol react reversibly to form methyl ethanoate and water. The following procedure was carried out by a chemistry student to estimate the equilibrium constant for this reaction.
- A mixture weighing 8.64 g was made by adding 0.08 mol of ethanoic acid and 0.12 mol of methanol. The mixture was left in a sealed glass syringe with a sliding piston which was placed in a water bath where its temperature was held steady at 60 °C for 3 hours. After this time, the temperature of the water bath was reduced to 20 °C. The syringe was left for 24 hours in the water bath. At this point, the system was assumed to be at equilibrium.
- The contents of the syringe were thoroughly mixed to form a homogeneous mixture and 1.0 g of the mixture was measured out and titrated with 0.40 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide delivered from a burette. A mean volume of 21.20 mL of sodium hydroxide solution was needed to reach the end-point of the titration, when it was assumed all of the ethanoic acid present in the mixture had reacted with the sodium hydroxide.

Would you expect the omission of concentrated $	ext{H}_2	ext{SO}_4$ in this investigation to affect the accuracy of the estimate for $K$? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer:
Yes — it is likely to make the estimate of $K$ inaccurate (too low).

A catalyst increases the rates of both the forward and reverse reactions equally; it does not change the position of equilibrium or the value of $K$, only how quickly equilibrium is reached. Without the catalyst, esterification is very slow, so after 3 hours at 60 °C and 24 hours at 20 °C the system may not actually have reached equilibrium.

The system approaches equilibrium from the left (starting with only acid and alcohol). If it has not reached equilibrium, too little ester and water have formed and too much $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ remains, so the titre is too high and the calculated $K$ is lower than the true value. (The very small value obtained, $K \approx 6 \times 10^{-3}$, compared with the accepted value of about 5 for esterification, is consistent with this.)

questions.question: Draw the functional group present in amides.
questions.answer:
The amide (carbamoyl) group: a carbonyl carbon bonded to a nitrogen,
$$\text{R}{-}\text{C}({=}\text{O}){-}\text{NH}_2 \qquad (\text{or } \text{R}{-}\text{C}({=}\text{O}){-}\text{NR}'\text{R}'' \text{ in general})$$
i.e. the $-\text{CONH}_2$ group in a primary amide.

questions.question:
Polyamides are a class of condensation polymer in which the monomers are joined by amide linkages, formed by reaction between an $-\text{NH}_2$ group on one molecule and a carboxyl group on another.

The structures below show two organic molecules, nicotinamide and ethanoic acid.

Could the reaction of the two molecules above result in the formation of a polyamide? Explain your answer.
questions.answer:
No.

Condensation polymerisation requires each monomer to have (at least) **two** reactive functional groups, one at each end, so that after one linkage forms each molecule can still react again and the chain can keep growing.

Nicotinamide has only one $-\text{NH}_2$ (in its $-\text{CONH}_2$ group) and ethanoic acid has only one $-\text{COOH}$ group. They could at most react once, eliminating water to form a single amide-linked molecule (a "dimer"); there would be no remaining reactive groups at either end, so no further molecules could join and no long polymer chain could form.

To make a polyamide, bifunctional monomers are needed, e.g. a diamine ($\text{H}_2\text{N}{-}\text{R}{-}\text{NH}_2$) with a dicarboxylic acid ($\text{HOOC}{-}\text{R}'{-}\text{COOH}$), as in nylon.

*Note: the paper's stem described polyamides as forming from "a compound with an amide group" and a carboxylic acid, and its answer refers to a "diamide"; polyamides form from amine (–NH₂) groups and carboxyl groups, so the stem has been reworded.*

questions.question:
An unknown compound was investigated using several techniques. The results are shown in the spectra below (infrared, mass, $^{1}$H NMR and $^{13}$C NMR spectra).

Draw and name the compound that was investigated. Support your answer with evidence from the spectra.
questions.answer:
**Infrared:** strong sharp absorption at ≈1725 cm$^{-1}$ → C=O (aldehyde or ketone). Absorptions at 2700–3000 cm$^{-1}$ → C–H. No broad absorption at 2500–3550 cm$^{-1}$ → no O–H (not an alcohol or acid); nothing at 3300–3500 cm$^{-1}$ → no N–H.

**Mass spectrum:** molecular ion at $m/z = 72$ → $M = 72$ g mol$^{-1}$, consistent with $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}$. Base peak at 43 → $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^+$, i.e. loss of CHO (29); peak at 29 → $\text{CHO}^+$; small peak at 57 → loss of $\text{CH}_3$.

**$^{13}$C NMR:** three signals → three carbon environments (so two carbons must be equivalent).
- ≈205 ppm: C=O of an aldehyde/ketone
- ≈41 ppm: CH carbon next to C=O
- ≈18 ppm: equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ carbons

**$^{1}$H NMR:** three environments, ratio 1 : 1 : 6.
- 9.6 ppm, doublet, 1H: aldehyde H (–CHO), split by 1 neighbouring H → next to a CH
- 2.4 ppm, multiplet, 1H: CH with 7 neighbouring H (1 CHO + 6 CH₃)
- 1.1 ppm, doublet, 6H: two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups, each next to the single CH

Putting the pieces together: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}{-}\text{CHO}$
$$\text{CH}_3{-}\underset{\displaystyle\text{CH}_3}{\underset{|}{\text{CH}}}{-}\text{C}({=}\text{O}){-}\text{H}$$
The compound is **2-methylpropanal**. This fits every spectrum: aldehyde C=O and no O–H (IR), $M = 72$ with $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^+$ (43) and $\text{CHO}^+$ (29) fragments (MS), 3 carbon environments including C=O at ≈205 ppm ($^{13}$C), and the 1 : 1 : 6 doublet/multiplet/doublet pattern ($^{1}$H).
